picks.title: A Buddhist Guide to How to Truly Love with Maria Heim
picks.summary:
Maria Heim is a professor of religion at Amherst College. Her new book, How to Truly Love: An Ancient Guide to a Life of Kindness, presents a fresh and accessible translation of a chapter from the Path of Purification, a meditation manual by the great 5th-century sage Buddhaghosa. Through a careful exploration of the brahmaviharas, or sublime attitudes, Buddhaghosa offers practical strategies for releasing anger and hatred and finding freedom.

picks.title: Metta as an Ethical Practice
picks.summary:
Metta as an Ethical PracticeRoy Wyman explores metta, or loving-kindness, as a practical antidote to ill will, shame, reactivity, and self-hatred. This talk moves from everyday mental habits to Buddhist teachings on community, authenticity, and emotional freedom, then closes with a guided loving-kindness meditation.This talk was given by Roy Wyman at Wild Heart Meditation Center in Nashville, TN. Support Wild Heart Meditation Center here: https://www.wildheartmeditationcenter.org/donateEnjoy!  
Wild Heart Meditation Center in a non-profit Buddhist community based in Nashville, TN. https://www.
picks.reason: Explores metta as a Buddhist ethical practice with meditation and community focus.

picks.title: Ep. 295 – Caverly Morgan
picks.summary: Caverly Morgan joins Sharon for episode 295 of the Metta Hour Podcast to talk about her book, The Heart of Who We Are.Caverly Morgan is a teacher of awakening, nonprofit founder, speaker, and author who blends the original spirit of Zen with a modern nondual and relational approach. Her practice began in 1995 and has included eight years of training in a silent Zen monastery. She has been teaching contemplative practice since 2001. Caverly supports others in remembering our true nature—not through more techniques or self-improvement strategies, but through presence, inquiry, and togetherness.
picks.reason: Zen teacher blends traditional and modern nondual approaches to awakening.

picks.title: Continuity of Mindfulness
picks.summary: We don't meditate to get good at meditation. Instead, our practice lays the ground for awareness which we, hopefully, carry throughout our days. Continuity of mindfulness is a phrase which conveys this idea. In this talk Mary talks about Thich Nhat Hanh's book, Peace is Every Breath, which brings practice down to the most mundane parts of our lives like brushing teeth and making breakfast. The sacred is right here all the time when we're aware.Recorded Sept. 12, 2026 in the virtual worldSend me a text with any questions or comments! Include your name and email if you would like a response - it
picks.reason: Talk on maintaining mindfulness continuously in daily life, inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh.

picks.title: 340 - Five Kinds of Appropriate Longing (1 of 2)
picks.summary: Many people think that the aim of Buddhism is let go of any kind of longing. However, without wholesome desires – to awaken, to act ethically, to honor your relationships, etc. – you wouldn't progress in practice. I discuss five kinds of appropriate longing based loosely on the Vajrayana teaching of the five wisdom energies.
picks.reason: Explores five kinds of wholesome longing important for Buddhist practice.

picks.title: Buddhist Chanting: Why We Do It | Benefits of Dhamma Recitation | Chant by Heart | Ajahn Dhammasiha
picks.summary: Chanting is an essential part of meditative practice in virtually all Buddhist traditions, and also in other religions. Ajahn Dhammasiha explains the powerful benefits we receive from diligently learning Buddhist chants by heart, from listening to them, and from reciting them regularly. Chanting the teaching of the Buddha develops samatha (tranquility) and samādhi, due to the calming and uplifting effect on our mind. If we understand the meaning of what we're chanting, it can also lead to profound insight (vipassana). Monks have attained enlightenment while chanting, teaching or listening to D
picks.reason: Explains chanting's meditative benefits and its role in Buddhist practice.

picks.title: Ep. 106 - An Interview with Zen teacher Mitra Bishop (Zen Podcast)
picks.summary: Our guest in this episode is Mitra Bishop Roshi. She received a B.A. from Indiana University, raised two children, and worked in graphic, interior, and architectural design for many years. She first encountered Buddhism while living in Asia. She was ordained at the Rochester Zen Center, where she lived and practiced for many years and received dharma transmission from Kapleau Roshi. Afterwards she traveled to Sogen-ji in Japan to practice under the guidance of the Zen master, Harada Shodo Roshi. She currently lives in New Mexico, where she has founded Mountain Gate. For more information about
